title: Hand Skeleton Anatomy
descriptor: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges, Carpal Tunnel & Fractures
intro: Each hand consists of 27 bones: eight carpal bones in the wrist, five metacarpal bones forming the palm and fourteen phalanges in the thumb and fingers. The carpal bones lie in two rows of four, and only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum take part in the wrist joint with the radius. The scaphoid is the carpal bone most often fractured, typically after a fall onto the hand.

sections.heading: Bones of the hand
sections.body: The eight carpal bones make up the wrist, the five metacarpal bones form the palm and the fourteen phalanges form the thumb and fingers. The metacarpals are numbered one to five starting from the thumb, and each is associated with a group of phalanges. The first metacarpal is freely mobile, whereas the other metacarpals are united as a group. The thumb has only two phalanges, a proximal and a distal, while each of the other four digits, from the index finger to the little finger, has a proximal, middle and distal phalanx. The knuckles are the metacarpophalangeal joints, where each metacarpal meets the proximal phalanx of its digit.

sections.heading: Carpal bones
sections.body: The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows of four, a proximal row and a distal row. Counting from the thumb side, the proximal row is the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform, and the distal row is the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate. Several names describe shape: scaphoid means boat-shaped, lunate moon-shaped, triquetrum three-cornered, pisiform pea-shaped, capitate head-shaped and hamate hooked. The pisiform can be felt as a bony bump at the medial base of the hand, and the hamate has a prominent bony extension on its anterior side, the hook of the hamate. Only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum take part in the wrist joint with the radius.

sections.heading: The carpal tunnel
sections.body: The flexor retinaculum, a fibrous band often called the transverse carpal ligament, forms the anterior roof of the carpal tunnel at the wrist. Deep to the band lie the four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, the four flexor digitorum profundus tendons, the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the median nerve. Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve at the wrist, causing hand pain, numbness and tingling in the area the nerve supplies. In longer-standing cases the muscle at the base of the thumb can waste. Thickening of the transverse carpal ligament and swelling of the tendons narrow the space and can compress the nerve, although in most cases the cause is unknown.

sections.heading: Fractures of the wrist and scaphoid
sections.body: The scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal bone, and NHS trust leaflets describe it as a small bone at the base of the thumb. A fall onto an outstretched hand is described as the most common cause of both scaphoid injuries and wrist fractures. A scaphoid injury typically causes pain and tenderness near the base of the thumb, and the wrist may swell, but most scaphoid fractures do not make the wrist look broken and many cause only minor symptoms. Some people also have difficulty gripping or twisting the wrist or thumb. NHS trust pages on wrist fractures describe immediate severe pain, swelling and often deformity of the wrist, painful movement, and sometimes tingling or numbness in the fingers. Wrist fractures are common in young children and older people. A wrist sprain can cause similar symptoms, and some suspected scaphoid injuries turn out to be sprains or bone bruises rather than breaks.

sections.heading: How scaphoid injuries are investigated
sections.body: A scaphoid fracture can be hard to diagnose because a stable fracture may be only a thin crack that is difficult to see on X-ray. In some people the fracture is not obvious on X-ray until some days after the injury. When the first X-ray is normal but a fracture is still suspected, clinicians re-examine the wrist and repeat the X-ray, and an MRI scan is requested if suspicion continues. Even without a visible fracture, a doctor who suspects one from the symptoms may treat the wrist as fractured to avoid complications. An X-ray is a quick, painless test that produces images of the inside of the body; the person needs to keep still, and more than one image may be taken from different angles.
